clue.text: Utterly exhausted result of 'mortal combat?

definitions.meaning: completely worn out, too tired to go on
after a fight to the death one fighter is lifeless and the other defeated

explanation.walkthrough: Read as two words, the second half describes the outcome of a duel: one party lifeless, the other beaten.
explanation.definitionFit: A colloquial term for complete fatigue; split in two it pairs 'killed' with 'defeated', the two outcomes of a fight.

clue.text: Can be taught to raise fish on French island

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising a word means writing it upwards, so it reads backwards

parts.note: the cod is a common food fish
ile is the French word for island

explanation.surface: Instructions for hoisting a catch ashore on an island off France.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'to raise' means write upwards, so the fish reads bottom to top; the French word for island then goes below it.
explanation.definitionFit: A docile pupil is teachable, willing to be instructed and managed.

clue.text: Reptile confounds a tall prince of 'opera

indicators.note: to confound is to throw into confusion, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
Prince Igor is the title role of Borodin's opera

explanation.surface: A creature bewilders a lofty royal from the opera house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confounds' mixes A, TALL and IGOR (Borodin's Prince Igor) together into the reptile.
explanation.definitionFit: The large American crocodilian is a reptile.

clue.text: Stormy, words of the deadpan comic, about fifty

indicators.note: the comedian's name goes about, or around, the Roman numeral

parts.note: Buster Keaton, the silent-film star famous for never smiling
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: A remark about a deadpan comedian's turbulent remarks when he reached fifty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts L (Roman fifty) inside BUSTER, the first name of Keaton, the 'Great Stone Face' of silent comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Bluster is loud, blustering talk, noisy and threatening speech likened to a gale.

clue.text: Colourful heroine, always cautious?

definitions.meaning: ... St Clare, heroine of Kathleen Winsor's racy novel Forever ..., also named after a colour
'always' is forever, and the traffic light between green and red signals caution, giving the novel's title

explanation.walkthrough: The second half spells out the novel's title Forever Amber: 'always' is forever, and in Britain the amber traffic light warns drivers to be cautious.
explanation.definitionFit: The name of a novel's heroine is also a yellowish-orange colour, the shade of the warning traffic light.

clue.text: American rodent used' to.. make Noah's ark

definitions.meaning: the burrowing pocket ... of North America
the Bible says the ark was built of ... wood

explanation.walkthrough: Genesis tells Noah to make the ark of 'gopher wood', so one word names both the burrower and the timber.
explanation.definitionFit: A North American burrowing animal shares its name with the timber of Genesis 6:14.

clue.text: Ancient. Mariner-one with skill and experience

parts.note: old means ancient
a hand is a sailor, a member of a ship's crew

explanation.surface: Coleridge's Ancient Mariner presented as a seasoned veteran.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface borrows Coleridge's poem 'The Rime of the Ancient Mariner'; the two words are taken separately, as OLD and HAND (a deckhand).
explanation.definitionFit: An expert veteran, someone long practised at a job, is called by this idiom.

clue.text: Bounders one takes to when in flight

definitions.meaning: cads or rotters, people who behave dishonourably

definitions.text: one takes to when in flight
definitions.meaning: to take to one's ... is to run away

explanation.walkthrough: 'flight' is fleeing, not flying: you 'take to your heels' when running off.
explanation.definitionFit: Cads are called this in slang, and the idiom 'take to one's heels' means to flee.

clue.text: Echo answers in'such a voice?

parts.note: an echo is a sound coming back, so it replies in a ringing, booming tone

explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue describes the deep, ringing kind of voice that an echo throws back.
explanation.definitionFit: A deep, ringing, reverberating tone is the kind that echoes.

clue.text: Platonic chat

parts.note: Plato wrote his philosophy as conversations between Socrates and others

explanation.walkthrough: 'Platonic' looks like 'non-romantic', but it means 'of Plato', whose works are written as conversations.
explanation.definitionFit: Plato's works take the form of conversations, the literary form named for talk between people.

clue.text: Eye trouble could exclude one from the snooker team

definitions.meaning: a defect of vision in telling hues apart

definitions.text: could exclude one from the snooker team
definitions.meaning: snooker is played with balls of many colours that a player must tell apart

explanation.walkthrough: Snooker, a British cue game, uses red balls and six other coloured balls, so a player who cannot tell colours apart would struggle.
explanation.definitionFit: Inability to distinguish hues is a vision defect, and would be fatal in a game played with coloured balls.

clue.text: Not such a heavyweight, but : a match-saver

definitions.meaning: weighing less, of a smaller weight class
a device that makes a flame, so you need not strike a match

explanation.walkthrough: 'match' suggests a sporting contest, but it is the thing you strike; a gas or petrol flame-maker saves using one.
explanation.definitionFit: The comparative of 'light' means weighing less, and a cigarette flame-maker replaces matches.

clue.text: Is this officer a man of affairs?

definitions.text: Is this officer a man of affairs?

parts.words: Is this officer a man of affairs?
parts.note: an officer who keeps contact between units has a title that also means a love affair

explanation.walkthrough: The officer who links two groups is named with a word that also means an illicit love affair; 'man of affairs' suggests business.
explanation.definitionFit: A liaison officer handles communication between groups, and the word also means a secret romance.

clue.text: Bird with heavenly body taking fish.

parts.note: a star is a heavenly body
ling is a long cod-like sea fish

explanation.surface: A bird in the sky alongside a star, catching fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking' joins the fish on after the heavenly body; LING is a cod-like fish common in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: The speckled songbird known for its huge flocks is a bird.

clue.text: A fraud whose admission of poverty takes in a saint

indicators.note: the confession surrounds the abbreviation, taking it inside

parts.note: saying 'I'm poor' confesses that one has no money

explanation.surface: A swindler whose plea of being broke cons a holy man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes in' means both 'deceives', fitting the fraud, and 'contains': I'M POOR surrounds ST.
explanation.definitionFit: A fake who pretends to be someone else is a fraud.

clue.text: Crazy, lady has no love lost for Thomas

indicators.note: crazy means wild or deranged, so the letters are disordered
the zero is taken away from the word no

parts.note: taken as written
love is zero in tennis, looking like the letter O

explanation.surface: A mad woman has lost interest in a man called Thomas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crazy' scrambles LADY to DYLA; NO with its O ('love', zero) 'lost' leaves N. Dylan Thomas was the Welsh poet.
explanation.definitionFit: The Welsh poet Dylan Thomas had this first name, so one name stands for the other.

clue.text: Tied up in the theatre?

parts.note: a surgeon in an operating theatre ties off blood vessels with thread

explanation.walkthrough: 'theatre' is the hospital operating theatre, not a stage; surgeons tie off vessels with thread there.
explanation.definitionFit: A surgical tie or thread binding a vessel gives this past participle meaning bound off.

clue.text: Sun, saved for summer

parts.note: clocks go forward in summer under the scheme that keeps evenings bright

explanation.walkthrough: The clue points to Daylight Saving Time, when clocks are put forward to keep summer evenings light.
explanation.definitionFit: Sunshine is natural light by day, and the summer clock change is called the saving of it.

clue.text: Flier going, for gold

parts.note: an archer's shaft flies towards the gold bullseye at the centre of the target

explanation.walkthrough: 'going for gold' sounds like an athlete chasing a medal; in archery the gold is the centre of the target.
explanation.definitionFit: The shaft shot from a bow is a flier, and in archery the target's middle ring is gold.

clue.text: Staked pay on one colour at roulette

parts.note: a wage is pay
roulette numbers are red or black

explanation.surface: A gambler puts a week's earnings on red at the casino.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface has the gambler betting their salary; the pieces are WAGE (pay) and RED.
explanation.definitionFit: To bet money on an outcome is to stake it.

clue.text: An old conjuring trick in -high esteem today,

definitions.meaning: the word once meant an illusion or sleight of hand, from Latin praestigiae
its modern sense is standing or renown

explanation.walkthrough: The word's original sense was a conjuror's illusion, from Latin praestigiae; only later did it mean renown.
explanation.definitionFit: Its modern sense is reputation or standing, and its old sense was a juggler's deception.

clue.text: Coach going by rail ?

definitions.meaning: a person who travels by train

explanation.walkthrough: 'Coach' looks like a bus or railway carriage; the second half reads the word as 'one who trains', that is, a train passenger.
explanation.definitionFit: A sports instructor has this title, and read literally it names one who travels by train.

clue.text: No minority parties

parts.note: minority is the state of being under age, so these people are past it

explanation.walkthrough: 'minority parties' looks political, but minority here is being legally under age, and 'parties' are people.
explanation.definitionFit: Grown-ups are those who are no longer minors, past the age of minority.

clue.text: Go miles. — astray to find China here-in France

indicators.note: to go astray is to wander off course, so the letters stray into a new order

explanation.surface: A traveller wanders off course looking for porcelain in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'astray' rearranges GO MILES. 'China' is porcelain, made in this French city.
explanation.definitionFit: A city in central France famous for its fine porcelain.

clue.text: A picture — still it isn't

parts.note: a moving picture is the opposite of a still photograph

explanation.walkthrough: 'still' reads as 'nevertheless', but it is a still photograph, which a moving picture is not.
explanation.definitionFit: A film is a moving picture, the opposite of a static one.

clue.text: Used explosive stroke or language in a bunker

definitions.text: Used explosive stroke or language in a bunker

parts.words: Used explosive stroke or language in a bunker
parts.note: a golfer escapes a sand trap with a forceful shot, and may also curse

explanation.walkthrough: A bunker is a golf sand trap: the 'explosion shot' out of it is called a blast, and a frustrated golfer may swear there.
explanation.definitionFit: The past tense covers both a forceful golf shot out of sand and an outburst of swearing.

clue.text: We hear the colonel is hold.. ing up a locomotive

indicators.note: signals that the word is said aloud, matching another spelling

parts.note: Colonel Bogey, the march, and the imaginary golfer of par play

explanation.surface: A railway mutiny in which an officer stops a train.
explanation.walkthrough: Colonel Bogey is a famous British march (and golf's imaginary par player); 'We hear' gives his name's sound, spelt as the wheel truck.
explanation.definitionFit: A wheeled undercarriage truck carries the weight of a locomotive or carriage.

clue.text: Crown representative makes. Pater' an army commander

parts.note: pater and governor are both old British slang for father
a general commands an army

explanation.surface: Father is presented as both viceroy and soldier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Governor' is old British slang for one's father, like 'pater' (Latin for father).
explanation.definitionFit: The monarch's representative in a Commonwealth country holds this title.

clue.text: River's the Wear ?

parts.note: the Wear and the Tweed are rivers in north-east England, and a cloth named after the latter is something to wear

explanation.walkthrough: The Wear is a river in north-east England, but here 'wear' means clothing: suits of cloth named for the river on the Scottish border.
explanation.definitionFit: Clothes of rough woollen cloth are named for the Border river.

clue.text: He takes, newly acquired harem to the islands

parts.note: wives just married are brides

explanation.surface: A sultan takes his new wives to an island retreat.
explanation.walkthrough: HE comes as written; a newly acquired harem is a group of brides. The islands lie off western Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: These are the Scottish island groups off the west coast.
